αὐτοῦ περιπα τήσαισαν. ... Ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ γάρ εἰσιν· ἐξέβαλον γὰρ τὸ φῶς ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν οἷς
ἔλεγεν· Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου. κ ʹ. Κατέδεται αὐτὸν πῦρ ἄκαυστον. Κατὰ δὲ τὸ
κρυπτόμενον, ἄκαυστον πῦρ 368 ἐστιν, ἤτοι τὸ κατὰ συνείδησιν, ἢ καὶ τὸ
ἀποκείμενον ἐν τοῖς μέλλουσιν δικαιωτη ρίοις. Καὶ ὡς ὑπὸ πυρὸς, φησὶν, ἀναλωθή
σεται, ἵνα εἴπῃ· Οὐδὲ ταφῆς ἀξιοῦται. κθʹ. Αὕτη ἡ μερὶς ἀνθρώπου ἀσεβοῦς παρὰ
Κυρίου, καὶ κτῆμα ὑπαρχόντων αὐτῷ παρὰ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου. Καθ' ἣν ἡ θεία κατ' αὐτοῦ
κινεῖται δίκη· εἴτε τοῦ ἐκ περιτομῆς διὰ Χριστὸν εἰς Θεὸν ἀσεβήσαντος, εἴτε τοῦ
παραδόξου, εἴθ' ὅπως ποτὲ ἀσεβοῦς, αὐτῷ μερίς ἐστιν ἡ δηλου μένη. –Μάνθανε τίς
ἐπίσκοπος ἐνθάδε ὠνο μάσθη· ὅτι Θεὸς ἐπίσκοπος εἴρηται, καὶ οἱ ἐπίσκοποι ἐκείνου
τὴν εἰκόνα παντὶ τῷ τρό πῳ φιλοτιμοῦνται, οἱ καλοὶ καὶ ἀγαθοὶ, φο ρεῖν. Καὶ ὥσπερ
ὁ μιμησάμενος εἰκόνα βα σιλικὴν, τιμᾶται ἐπὶ τῷ καλῶς αὐτὴν μι μήσασθαι· τιμᾶται
δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ αὐτὴν κεκοσμηκέναι· οὕτως μακάριος ἐπίσκοπος ὁ νοήσας τὸν
ἀληθινὸν ἐπίσκοπον, καὶ ζηλῶν αὐτὸν, καὶ γινόμενος ὡς ἐν ἀνθρώποις Θεὸς, ἢ ὁ
ἔχων ἐπίσκοπον τὸν ποιοῦντα αὐτὸν ἀληθῶς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἐπίσκοπον, ᾧ ἡ δόξα
καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. Κεφ. ΚΑʹ, ιαʹ, ιβʹ. Τὰ δὲ παιδία
αὐτῶν προσπαίζουσι, ἀναλαβόντες ψαλτήριον καὶ κιθάραν, καὶ εὐφραίνονται φωνῇ
ψαλμοῦ. Ἰδοὺ καὶ τὰ μωρὰ παιδία αὐτῶν ἑαυτοῖς προσπαίζονται. Λέγουσι γὰρ αὐτοὶ
ψαλμοὺς Οὐαλεντινοῦ καὶ ᾠδὰς Βασιλείδου, καὶ τοι αῦτά τινα φθέγγονται,
εὐφραινόμενοι φωνῇ ψαλμοῦ. 369 Κεφ. ΚΒʹ, βʹ. Πότερον οὐχὶ ὁ Κύριός ἐσ τιν ὁ
διδάσκων σύνεσιν καὶ ἐπιστήμην; Ἴδωμεν τί φησιν ὁ Ἐλιφὰζ πρὸς τὸν δίκαιον·
Πότερον κτλ ... Τοῦτο τοῦ Ἰὼβ εἰ ρηκότος, συντρέχει τῷ λόγῳ καὶ ὁ Ἐλιφὰζ, καί
φησιν· Οἶδα κἀγὼ ὅτι τοὺς λόγους, δι' ὧν ὁ μέν τις ὢν ἀσεβὴς εὐθυνεῖται, ὁ δὲ
κολάζεται, ὁ μόνος σοφὸς οἶδε Θεός· οἶδα δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ὅτι Θεὸς μὲν, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς
ἔφης, τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἐστι δοτήρ· ἡ δὲ κακία τὰς κολάσεις δίδωσιν. –Ὑγιὲς τὸ δόγμα ... –
̓Επιστήμη, ἡ περιοχὴ τῶν ὡσαύτως ἐχόντων θεωρία, σύνεσις δὲ ἡ διάκρισις. εʹ.
Πότερον οὐχ ἡ κακία σου ἐστὶ πολλὴ, ἀναρίθμητοι δέ σου εἰσιν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι; Εἰκότως
οὖν φημὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς γεγονέναι σε ἄδικον, ἐπεὶ πάσχεις τοιαῦτα, οἷα οὐδεὶς τῶν
κακῶν, ἀλλ' ἐν τούτοις γεγεννῆσθαι, δη λονότι πλείονα κακίαν [τῶν κακῶν] ὑπὲρ
τοὺς ἄλλους ἐσχηκέναι. Κακία ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ κακὴ ἕξις, οἷον λύπης, ὀργῆς, καὶ ἐπι
θυμία ἀπρεπής· ἀμαρτία δὲ ἡ ἐνέργεια· διὸ πρῶτον εἶπεν τὴν κακίαν, εἶτα τὴν ἁμαρ
τίαν, τὴν μὲν πολλὴν, τὰς δὲ ἀναριθμήτους. Πάνυ πολλοὺς ὁρῶ ἁμαρτωλοὺς, καὶ
οὐδεὶς αὐτῶν τηλικούτοις περιπέπτωκεν οἷος σύ. 370 Εἰκὸς γὰρ, διὰ τὸ ἀναρίθμητόν
σου τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ τὸ πλῆθός σου τῶν πταισ μάτων, ταῦτά σοι
ἐπεληλυθέναι. ʹ. Ἠνεχύραζες δὲ τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου διακε νῆς· ἀμφίασιν δὲ γυμνῶν
ἀφείλου. Πρόσχωμεν, οἱ τοκογλύφοι· μήποτε ἐνε χυράζωμεν διακενῆς. Ὠφέλιμα τὰ
ῥήματα, κατὰ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ λέγειν κατὰ λόγον ἁμαρ τήματα ἀληθῶς, ψεκτῶς
γινομένων ἐν ἀν θρώποις. Ὑπολαμβάνει τοῦτο ὁ Ἐλίφας περὶ τοῦ Ἰὼβ, ἐπειδὴ ᾔδει
αὐτὸν πλούσιον, καὶ ὑπώπτευσεν ἀπὸ τοιούτων τινῶν πόρων πλου τεῖν αὐτόν· διό
φησιν· Ἠνεχύραζες διακενῆς, τουτέστιν μηδὲν ἐποφειλόμενος. –Εἰ δὲ ἐδάνεισα, καὶ
μὴ πιστεύων τῷ δανεισαμένῳ, ἔλαβον ἐνήχυρον ἀξιόχρεων πρὸς ὃ ἔχρησα, ἔλαβον
ἐνήχυρον, οὐ διακενῆς δέ. Εἰ μέντοι, συκοφαντῶν αὐτὸν, καὶ λέγων ὀφείλειν μοι μὴ
δυνάμενον ἀποδοῦναι, ἀπαιτῶ καὶ λαμ βάνω, ἐνήχυρον [λαμβάνω] διακενῆς.
Προσεπιτείνει δὲ πάλιν, ἄλλην αὐτοῦ ἁ μαρτίαν οἰόμενος γεγονέναι. Ἔστι ποτὲ λα
βεῖν ἀμφιάσματα, οὐ τοῦ γυμνοῦ, ἀλλὰ πλου σίου, ἔχοντος ἕτερα ἀποκείμενα
ἐνδύματα πολλὰ λαβεῖν, τρία δή· ὧν τῶν πολλῶν ἐκεῖ ἔλαβον ἀμφίασιν· ἄλλα
γυμνοῦ, ἄλλα πλου σίου. Ἐὰν μέντοι γε χιτῶνα ἔχῃ τις ἕνα, καὶ τοῦτον τὸν χιτῶνα,
προφάσει τοῦ ἀπαι τεῖν τὸ ἐμὸν, ἐκδύσω, μὴ ἐλεήσας ἐκεῖνον τὸν γυμνὸν, ἀμφίασιν
τοῦ γυμνοῦ ἀφειλόμην. Πολλὰ δὲ τοιαῦτα ἐν ἡμῖν γίνεται, ὅταν δανείζωμεν, ὅταν
πρὸς ὀφειλέτας ἐρχώμεθα· πολλάκις ὀφειλέτης ἡμῶν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν πέ νεται, μὴ
δυνάμενος ἀποδοῦναι· καὶ ἡμεῖς τὰ σπλάγχνα ἡμῶν ἀποκλείσαντες, ἀνελεεῖς καὶ
ὠμοὶ γινόμεθα, μὴ βλέποντες ὅτι γυ ναῖκα τρέφει καὶ τέκνα, καὶ μόλις τρέφεται 371
ἀπὸ τῶν ποριζομένων αὐτῷ ὀλίγων ὀβολῶν· ἀπαιτοῦμεν πικρῶς, ἔσθ' ὅτε καὶ
περισσὰ ἔχοντες παρ' ἑαυτοῖς. Τοιαῦτα γίνεται ἐν ταῖς πικραῖς ἀπαιτή σεσιν, ἐνίοτε
pass_a_gloss: (Continues the lemma of Job 20:25 from the previous section:) ... his [dwellings] may they walk about. ... For they are in not-knowing; for they threw out the light from themselves, those to whom he used to say: I am the light of the world. Verse 26 (label printed 'κ ʹ'; the stigma is lost). An unburnt fire will eat him down. According to what is hidden, the unburnt fire is either the one in conscience, or also the one stored up in the future places of punishment. And as by fire, he says, he will be used up, so that he may say: he is not even counted worthy of a burial. Verse 29. This is the share of an impious man from the Lord, and a possession of the things belonging to him from the overseer (bishop). According to which the divine justice is moved against him: whether of the one from circumcision who acted impiously toward God on account of Christ, or of the one of strange opinion, or of one impious in whatever way, for him is the share being shown. Learn who has been named bishop here: that God is called bishop, and the bishops, the fine and good ones, are eager in every manner to wear that one's image. And just as the one who imitated a royal image is honored on account of imitating it well, and is honored also on account of having decorated it, so blessed is a bishop who has perceived the true bishop, and is zealous for him, and becomes as God among humans; or the one having as bishop the one making him truly a bishop in Christ Jesus, to whom the glory and the might into the ages of the ages. Amen. Chapter 21, verses 11, 12. And their little children play, having taken up harp and cithara, and are made glad by a voice of a psalm. Look, also their foolish little children play at themselves. For they themselves say psalms of Valentinus and songs of Basilides, and utter some such things, being made glad by a voice of a psalm. Chapter 22, verse 2. Is it not the Lord who is the one teaching understanding and knowledge? Let us see what Eliphaz says toward the righteous man: Is it not, and so on ... Job having said this, Eliphaz also runs together with the statement, and says: I also know that the reasons through which one man, being impious, thrives (printed form read as the verb 'to thrive'), and another is punished, the only wise God knows; and I know also this, that God, as you yourself also said, is the giver of the good things; but wickedness gives the punishments. Healthy is the doctrine ... Knowledge: the embracing contemplation of the things being in the same state; and understanding: the discerning. Verse 5. Is not your wickedness much, and your sins are uncountable? Reasonably then I say that you have not simply become unjust, since you suffer such things as none of the bad, but have been born in these, clearly having had more wickedness than the others [of the bad]. Wickedness is in the soul a bad habit, as of grief, of anger, and unfitting desire; and sin the working; therefore he said first the wickedness, then the sin, the one much, the others uncountable. Very many sinners I see, and none of them has fallen into such great things as you. For it is fitting that because of the uncountable [number] of your sins and the multitude of your falls these things have come upon you. Verse 6 (label printed 'ʹ' alone; the stigma is lost). And you took pledges of your brothers for nothing; and the covering of naked men you took away. Let us pay attention, the usurers: lest we take pledges for nothing. Profitable the words; according to this it is to speak in reason sins truly, of things happening blameworthily among humans. Eliphas supposes this about Job, since he knew him to be rich, and suspected him to be rich from some such resources; therefore he says: You took pledges for nothing, that is, nothing being owed in addition. But if I lent, and not trusting the one who borrowed, took a pledge worth the debt toward what I lent, I took a pledge, but not for nothing. If however, slandering him and saying that he owes me, being unable to repay, I demand and take, I take a pledge for nothing. And he stretches further again, thinking another sin of his to have happened. It is possible at times to take clothes, not of the naked, but of a rich man, who has other many garments stored up, to take, three indeed; of which many I took a covering there; one thing of the naked, another of the rich. If however someone has one tunic, and this tunic, on pretext of demanding back my own, I strip off, not having pitied that naked man, I took away the covering of the naked. And many such things happen among us, whenever we lend, whenever we go toward debtors; often our debtor is poor to excess, not able to repay; and we, having shut off our inward parts, become unmerciful and raw, not seeing that he nourishes a wife and children, and is scarcely nourished from the few obols procured for him; we demand back bitterly, sometimes even having surplus beside ourselves. Such things happen in the bitter demandings, sometimes (runs on into the next section)
pass_b_english: “… may walk about” (Job 20:25). … For they are in ignorance: they cast the light away from themselves, they to whom he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

“An unkindled fire will devour him” (Job 20:26). In the hidden sense, the unkindled fire is either the fire of conscience, or else the fire laid up in the places of punishment to come. And he will be consumed as by fire, he says, meaning: he is not even thought worthy of burial.

“This is the portion of an ungodly man from the Lord, and the possession of his goods from the Bishop” (Job 20:29). It is the portion by which divine justice is set in motion against him. Whether he is the man from the circumcision who has been ungodly toward God because of Christ, or the man of strange opinions, or ungodly in any way whatever, the portion here declared is his. Learn who is here named Bishop: God is called Bishop, and the bishops, the good and noble ones, make it their ambition in every way to bear his image. And just as one who copies a royal image is honored for copying it well, and honored also for having adorned it, so blessed is the bishop who has understood the true Bishop, and emulates him, and becomes as God among men; or the one who has as his bishop him who makes him truly a bishop in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the might to the ages of ages. Amen.

“And their children play, taking up psaltery and lyre, and they rejoice at the sound of a psalm” (Job 21:11-12). See, their foolish children too are playing among themselves. For they recite psalms of Valentinus and odes of Basilides, and they utter such things, rejoicing at the sound of a psalm.

“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” Let us see what Eliphaz says to the righteous man: “Is it not,” and so on … When Job had said this, Eliphaz too falls in with the argument and says: I too know that the reasons why one man, though ungodly, prospers and another is punished are known to God, who alone is wise. And I know this as well: God, as you yourself said, is the giver of good things, but wickedness deals out the punishments. The teaching is sound … Knowledge is the comprehensive contemplation of things that always hold the same way; understanding is discernment.

“Is not your wickedness great, and your sins without number?” (Job 22:5). With reason, then, I say that you have not simply become unjust, since you suffer such things as none of the wicked suffer, but that you were born in these things; plainly, you have had more wickedness than the others among the wicked. Wickedness is a bad state in the soul, as of grief or of anger, and unseemly desire; sin is its activity. That is why he named wickedness first and then sin, calling the one great and the others numberless. I see a great many sinners, and none of them has fallen into such evils as you have. For it is likely that these things have come upon you because of your numberless sins and the multitude of your stumbles.

“You took pledges from your brothers for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing” (Job 22:6). Let us take heed, we who lend at interest, that we never take pledges for nothing. The words are useful: in this respect it is reasonable to speak truly of sins, of things done blameworthily among men. Eliphaz suspects this of Job because he knew he was rich, and he suspected that he had grown rich from some such sources. So he says, “You took pledges for nothing,” that is, when nothing was owed you. If I lent, and, not trusting the borrower, took a pledge worth what I lent, I took a pledge, but not for nothing. But if I bring a false charge against a man, saying that he owes me when he cannot repay, and I demand and take, then I take a pledge for nothing.

He presses further again, supposing that another sin of his had taken place. One may sometimes take garments, not from the naked, but from a rich man who has many other clothes laid by, and take, say, three; from those many I took clothing there. The naked man's case is one thing, the rich man's another. But if someone has one tunic, and on the pretext of demanding what is mine I strip that tunic off him, without pity for that naked man, I have taken away the clothing of the naked.

Many such things happen among us when we lend, when we go after debtors. Often our debtor is poor beyond measure and cannot repay; and we shut up our hearts and become pitiless and cruel, not seeing that he feeds a wife and children and barely feeds himself on the few obols he earns. We demand payment bitterly, sometimes even when we have more than enough laid by. Such things happen in bitter demands for payment; sometimes …

lemmas.gloss: usurer, one who lends at interest

choices.choice: 'the light has emanated from within themselves' -> 'they cast the light away from themselves' (ἐξέβαλον); 'judgments that await the righteous' -> 'places of punishment to come' (δικαιωτήρια); 'a possession held by those under the bishop' -> 'the possession of his goods from the Bishop'; 'O engravers' -> 'we who lend at interest' (τοκογλύφοι); 'you left nothing unpaid' -> 'when nothing was owed you'; 'that is not true lending' -> 'I took a pledge, but not for nothing'; 'a woman must feed children' -> 'he feeds a wife and children'.
The lemma's ἐπίσκοπος (God) and the church's ἐπίσκοποι are one word, and the comment turns on that; rendered 'Bishop' (God) and 'bishop(s)' throughout rather than 'Overseer'.

'κ ʹ' is κϛʹ (stigma lost; the words are LXX 20:26). Bare 'ʹ' before 'Ἠνεχύραζες' is ϛʹ (Job 22:6). Opening words '... αὐτοῦ περιπατήσαισαν' finish the Job 20:25 lemma begun at the end of u01-rem-early.
'εὐθυνεῖται' read as εὐθηνεῖται 'prospers': the contrast is with 'another is punished'; 'is called to account' would not contrast. The old English 'is corrected' is replaced.
'εἴτε τοῦ παραδόξου' rendered 'the man of strange opinions'; the word is unusual for a heretic and may be corrupt (perhaps for ἑτεροδόξου).

'Ὠφέλιμα τὰ ῥήματα, κατὰ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ λέγειν κατὰ λόγον ἁμαρτήματα ἀληθῶς, ψεκτῶς γινομένων' and 'λαβεῖν, τρία δή· ὧν τῶν πολλῶν ἐκεῖ ἔλαβον ἀμφίασιν· ἄλλα γυμνοῦ, ἄλλα πλουσίου' are rendered closely; meaning uncertain, no sense added.
'[τῶν κακῶν]' (bracketed in the print) rendered 'among the wicked'; 'γεγεννῆσθαι' rendered 'were born in these things'.
'Basileidus' corrected to Basilides; Eliphas/Eliphaz printed both ways, Eliphaz used.
Review 2026-11-11: not printed inline; the LXX lemma and KJV Job 22:2 share only the verse number. Kept in added_allusions.
